nodes.title: Our Company
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its evolution from PC graphics into GPU-accelerated computing for gaming, AI, scientific computing, data science, autonomous vehicles, robotics, and AR/VR. It outlines its unified, developer-supported platform strategy, innovation and R&D history, and adoption across gaming, research, cloud services, enterprises, and industries. The text gives its headquarters and incorporation history, reports termination of the proposed Arm acquisition and a planned $1.36 billion charge, and describes its Graphics and Compute & Networking segments. It introduces four core markets—Gaming, Data Center, Professional Visualization, and Automotive—and details gaming products and RTX/DLSS technology, plus Data Center hardware, software, applications, and AI, machine learning, and HPC workloads.

nodes.title: NVIDIA Business, Markets, and Gaming
key_items: Termination of the Arm Share Purchase Agreement
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s company background is followed by the terminated Arm acquisition, its regulatory cause, and a planned $1.36 billion write-off. The page outlines its Graphics and Compute & Networking segments, and its four markets: Gaming, Data Center, Professional Visualization, and Automotive. It describes gaming’s growth drivers, GPU- and software-based enhancements including RTX ray tracing and DLSS, and gaming products such as GeForce GPUs, GeForce NOW, SHIELD, and console platforms and services.

nodes.title: Data Center
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s energy-efficient GPUs, DPUs, interconnects, systems, CUDA platform, libraries, tools, frameworks and services accelerate AI, analytics, graphics and scientific computing across data centers and edge environments. The text explains deep learning, machine learning and HPC, and describes NVIDIA’s industry partnerships and AI applications. It covers GPU availability in servers, clouds and DGX systems; HGX, EGX and AGX designs; BlueField DPUs, DOCA software and planned CPUs; and its full-stack software, NGC catalog, deployment options, and standalone enterprise products for AI, fleet and workflow management, and virtual GPU workloads.

nodes.title: Professional Visualization
nodes.summary: NVIDIA serves professional visualization by optimizing GPU solutions with software partners to improve workflows in design, manufacturing, and digital content creation. Its RTX platform enables real-time ray-traced, photorealistic rendering, supported by leading applications. Physically based rendering helps designers create realistic digital images. Omniverse provides 3D simulation and collaboration for enterprise subscribers and individual users; Omniverse, VR, and AR support applications including virtual showrooms, surgical training, architectural walkthroughs, and historical recreations.

nodes.title: Automotive
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s Automotive business includes cockpit AV platforms, AI cockpit and infotainment solutions, and development agreements. Its DRIVE end-to-end offerings support autonomous driving and driver assistance, developed with hundreds of automotive ecosystem partners. The unified architecture uses GPUs to train neural networks and DRIVE Hyperion—DRIVE AGX hardware, reference sensors, and modular software—to run perception, planning, and control. Planned software includes DRIVE Chauffeur for autonomous driving, mapping, and parking, and DRIVE Concierge for in-vehicle and conversational AI. DRIVE combines deep learning, sensor fusion, and surround vision, scales from highway automation to driverless systems, and uses the Orin SoC for multi-sensor processing and DRIVE AutoPilot, including cockpit visualization. DRIVE Constellation and DRIVE Sim provide data-center simulation for testing and validation. The software-defined platform supports ongoing development and over-the-air updates.

nodes.title: Business Strategies
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s strategies include advancing its full-stack accelerated computing platform across gaming, data center, professional visualization, and automotive through shared GPU/CUDA technology and continued performance gains; extending AI leadership with end-to-end hardware, software, broad industry availability, developer and education ecosystems; advancing graphics through GPUs, optimized software, creative and collaboration tools, and cloud access; developing a safety-focused, end-to-end autonomous-driving platform with partners, including training and simulation; and expanding technology reach through IP licensing and custom development.

nodes.title: Sales and Marketing
nodes.summary: NVIDIA describes its global sales and marketing strategy, partner ecosystem, technical design support, developer engagement, early-access programs, and AI training, as well as sales through e-tail, cloud, and enterprise channels. It outlines product seasonality and fiscal 2022 supply constraints. Its fabless manufacturing model relies on suppliers and subcontractors for fabrication, assembly, testing, packaging, components, and logistics, with advance orders and deposits used to secure capacity. Competition is intense and shaped by performance, product breadth, software, distribution, manufacturing, pricing, and system costs; rivals include GPU, SoC, AI-computing, and high-performance interconnect providers.

nodes.title: Market Channels, Seasonality, and Manufacturing
nodes.summary: NVIDIA sells through partners, e-tailers, and directly to cloud and enterprise customers as its business expands beyond gaming into platforms, systems, and software. Consumer revenue typically strengthens in the fiscal second half; notebook and console products often peak in quarters two and three, though fiscal 2022 supply constraints disrupted historical patterns. NVIDIA uses a fabless model, relying on suppliers and subcontractors for wafers, assembly, testing, packaging, components, and finished products while focusing on design, quality, marketing, and support. It sometimes secures supply early through non-cancellable orders, premiums, and deposits. The text outlines key suppliers and the flow of products through quality checks, contract manufacturers, distributors, and end customers.

nodes.title: Competition
nodes.summary: The text describes intense, rapidly changing competition in GPUs, accelerated computing, AI processors, SoCs, and high-performance interconnects. Competitiveness depends on performance, product range, customer access, software and standards support, manufacturing, pricing, quality, and anticipating demand; rivals may have greater resources, and competition may grow. It lists competitors across chipmakers, internet companies, SoC suppliers, and interconnect providers. IP protection relies on patents, trademarks, trade secrets, agreements, licenses, and foreign laws, whose protections vary; patent terms, protection priorities, and continued third-party licensing are noted. Government regulations and acquisition reviews may raise costs or harm results; the failed Arm acquisition is expected to incur a $1.36 billion charge. Existing compliance has not materially affected operations, but numerous current and future rules could adversely affect the business.

nodes.title: Competition, Intellectual Property, and Government Regulation
nodes.summary: The page outlines competition from chip, computing, automotive, and interconnect suppliers and in-house design teams, noting competitors may have greater resources and adaptability. It describes IP protections, patent coverage and expiration dates, risks of weaker foreign enforcement, criteria for seeking protection, and ongoing third-party licensing. It also covers worldwide regulatory obligations, acquisition-review risks, the terminated Arm deal and expected $1.36 billion charge, current compliance impacts, and potential future costs and business effects across numerous regulatory areas.

nodes.title: NVIDIA ESG, Climate and Workforce
nodes.summary: NVIDIA integrates ESG principles across its business, with Board committee oversight and annual priority reviews; further details and ESG risks are identified in its CSR materials and SEC risk factors. It assesses climate impacts and risks, reports environmental metrics, targets 100% renewable electricity by fiscal 2025, and emphasizes GPU energy efficiency, including strong Green500 results. It plans Earth-2 for climate modeling. As of January 2022, NVIDIA had 22,473 employees across 32 countries and focuses on attracting, developing, and retaining talent. Recruitment draws on varied strategies and global sources, with employee referrals accounting for over 39% of new hires.

nodes.title: Development and Retention
nodes.summary: The text describes employee development and retention through training, coaching, learning resources, tuition support, internal mobility, and mentoring for women and underrepresented groups; engagement surveys and feedback channels; and a 4.9% FY2022 turnover rate. It covers performance-based equity compensation, health, financial, and tailored benefits, and diversity and inclusion initiatives, including recruiting, development, resource groups, training, and progress tracking, alongside workforce demographics. It also outlines COVID-19 safety measures, office access protocols, and work-from-home support.

nodes.title: Employee Development, Compensation, Benefits, and Inclusion
nodes.summary: The page describes employee development through tuition reimbursement, career coaching, mentoring, and feedback channels, reporting 4.9% turnover in fiscal 2022. It outlines performance-linked equity and benefits supporting physical, mental, and financial well-being, tailored to employee needs. It also details diversity and inclusion commitments, recruiting and development initiatives, resource groups, training, and progress measurement, alongside workforce gender and U.S. racial and ethnic representation figures.

nodes.title: Health and COVID-19
nodes.summary: During fiscal 2022 and the COVID-19 pandemic, the company prioritized employee and family health and safety through global protocols, social distancing at essential open sites, and metric- and government-guided office access. Employee support included work-from-home resources and expense reimbursement; enhanced health coverage, COVID-19 testing and vaccine support, mental health and virtual care, and COVID-19 care; remote-management learning resources; and virtual social connection. The company will maintain flexible work and company-wide rest days.

title: ITEM 1A. RISK FACTORS

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Industry and Markets If we fail to meet the evolving needs of our markets, or to identify new products, services or technologies, our revenue and financial results may be adversely impacted.
nodes.summary: NVIDIA warns that known or unforeseen risks could harm its business, finances, results, or reputation and reduce its stock price, potentially causing investors to lose some or all of their investment. Its Gaming, Data Center, Professional Visualization, and Automotive markets change rapidly. Success depends on anticipating needs and trends, developing and gaining adoption for products and technologies, expanding ecosystems, forecasting demand, meeting changing safety and compliance standards, managing lifecycles, scaling infrastructure and capabilities, and making substantial investments. New-market investments may not yield revenue for years or at all. Design wins can take time, depend on anticipating customer requirements, and do not guarantee revenue; missed wins may limit future opportunities. Changing standards or disruptive technologies may make products incompatible or noncompliant, while failing to adapt strategy to evolving markets could harm the business.

nodes.title: Competition in our current and target markets could prevent us from growing our revenue.
nodes.summary: Competition in current and target markets could constrain growth as offerings, standards, customer needs, entrants and consolidation evolve. Competitors may offer cheaper or superior products and have advantages in fabrication, experience, customers, IP, designs, resources, market responsiveness and access to constrained supply. In networking, customers that are also chip and switch suppliers may use licensed technology and transferred IP to develop replacement solutions. Failure to compete, adapt, and introduce relevant offerings could reduce demand and revenue.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Demand, Supply and Manufacturing If we fail to estimate customer demand properly, there may be a mismatch between supply and demand, and our financial results could be harmed.
nodes.summary: The text warns that inaccurate demand forecasts can cause shortages, excess inventory, lost sales, market share, customer trust, and financial harm. Demand is affected by product launches, competitors, channel partners, cryptocurrency mining and policy or technology changes, gray-market resale, and pandemic-driven behavior; LHR GPUs and CMP may not manage mining demand as intended. Long manufacturing lead times and semiconductor constraints require advance commitments, inventory, deposits, and premiums. Overestimates can cause write-downs, lower prices, and margin impacts; underestimates may leave partners unable to supply orders promptly or economically. Long-term non-cancellable orders may worsen excess inventory and costs if demand falls or competitors serve it.

nodes.title: We depend on third parties and their technology to manufacture, assemble, test, package or design our products, which reduces our control over product quantity and quality, manufacturing yields, development, enhancement and product delivery schedule and could harm our business.
nodes.summary: The company relies on third parties for semiconductor fabrication, assembly, testing, packaging, and design tools, limiting its control over supply, quality, yields, development, and delivery. Available tools may not support product requirements, and capacity commitments may be insufficient. Risks include inaccurate or delayed orders, supply or capacity shortfalls, higher prices, manufacturing or process-technology failures, reliance on a limited supplier base, costs and delays when changing suppliers, competitors receiving priority, and low yields. These issues could hinder customer demand and scaling, and harm operations, margins, revenue, and financial results.

nodes.title: If our products contain significant defects, we could incur significant expenses to remediate such defects, our reputation could be damaged, and we could lose market share.
nodes.summary: Complex hardware and software may have defects, security vulnerabilities, failures, or poor performance due to design, manufacturing, materials, packaging, or system use, with risks rising in new markets, applications, technologies, and releases. Problems may emerge only after shipment and expose customers to malicious attacks or damage integrated products and end users. Consequences include warranty, support, repair, replacement, recall, inventory write-off, customer reimbursement, and engineering diversion costs; reduced market acceptance, design wins, customer and partner relationships, brand perception, revenue, margins, and financial results; and costly product-liability claims. Insurance may be inadequate or unavailable on acceptable terms.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Our Global Operating Business We are subject to risks and uncertainties associated with international operations, including adverse economic conditions, which may harm our business.
nodes.summary: The company’s worldwide operations, overseas manufacturing and 84% non-U.S. revenue expose it to political, economic, legal, cultural, currency, capital-market and catastrophic-event risks. Recessions, policy uncertainty, inflation and other economic changes may raise costs, reduce margins and demand, disrupt suppliers and customers, cause insolvencies or industry consolidation, constrain forecasting and financing, and increase credit, liquidity, counterparty and asset risks. Its Israeli engineering, sales-support and manufacturing operations may also face boycotts or restrictions on business with Israel, harming results.

nodes.title: Climate change may have a long-term impact on our business.
nodes.summary: Climate change could disrupt the company and its customers, partners, and suppliers through extreme weather, unreliable water or energy, wildfire-related power shutoffs affecting California offices and data centers, supply-chain and infrastructure damage, and political instability—causing operational interruptions, attrition, losses, and higher costs. Insurance may not cover losses because of limits, deductibles, exclusions, or insurer failure. Climate laws, regulations, and lawsuits could raise manufacturing, materials, capital, compliance, and energy costs, require operational or product-design changes, and cause reputational harm, litigation, or supply disputes. The company may miss its 2025 renewable-electricity goal or incur unexpected costs to meet it. Climate-driven preferences may reduce demand for energy-intensive products such as GPUs or increase expectations for product efficiency.

nodes.title: We may not be able to realize the potential benefits of business investments or acquisitions, and we may not be able to successfully integrate acquisition targets, which could hurt our ability to grow our business, develop new products or sell our products.
nodes.summary: Acquisitions and strategic investments may fail to deliver expected benefits or integrate successfully, limiting growth, product development and sales and harming financial results. Risks include resource and opportunity costs, delays or failed regulatory approvals, lost talent, changing technology, impaired deal prospects, public-investment volatility, and a $1.36 billion planned write-off after NVIDIA and SoftBank terminated the proposed Arm acquisition. Other risks include integration and retention difficulties; diverted resources; liabilities, amortization and impairments; operational and financial-system coordination; uncertain returns, approvals or financing; stock-price, fee, fine and reputational harm; litigation; debt, dilution and variable consideration; economic changes; due-diligence failures; and damaged or lost employee, vendor and customer relationships.

nodes.title: System security and data protection breaches, as well as cyber-attacks, could disrupt our operations, reduce our expected revenue and increase our expenses, which could adversely affect our stock price and damage our reputation.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks, including a 2022 breach involving stolen credentials and leaked proprietary source code, and explains potential operational, financial, legal, regulatory, and reputational harms; third-party and supply-chain exposure; recovery limitations; and ongoing security costs and challenges. It also describes disruption risks from disasters, climate and resource constraints, outages, conflict, and political instability, including geographic and supplier concentration. Other risks include reliance on a few customers and partners whose orders may change or be lost, and difficulty attracting, retaining, motivating, and succession-planning executives and skilled, diverse employees.

nodes.title: Operational, Customer, and Talent Risks
key_items: Business disruptions could harm our operations, lead to a decline in revenue and increase our costs.
We receive a significant amount of our revenue from a limited number of customers and our revenue could be adversely affected if we lose or are prevented from selling to any of these customers.
If we are unable to attract, retain and motivate our executives and key employees, our business may be harmed.
nodes.summary: The page describes risks from natural disasters, extreme weather, infrastructure and technology outages, geopolitical conflict, and other disruptions that could interrupt operations and supply chains, raise costs, reduce revenue, and harm results and reputation. Revenue concentration among a few customers and partners creates exposure to order changes, cancellations, competition, trade restrictions, and collection difficulties. It also explains that difficulty attracting, retaining, and motivating executives and employees—including diverse talent—could increase costs, impair strategy, and reduce acquisition benefits.

nodes.title: Business Systems and COVID-19 Risks
key_items: Our business is dependent upon the proper functioning of our business processes and information systems and modification or interruption of such systems may disrupt our business, processes and internal controls.
The COVID-19 pandemic continues to impact our business and could materially adversely affect our financial condition and results of operations.
nodes.summary: The company depends on reliable business processes and information systems, including internal financial controls; ERP implementation and control failures could disrupt operations, reporting, growth, and compliance, while material weaknesses may trigger costs, restatements, investor concern, stock declines, restricted market access, or regulatory action. COVID-19 affects the company and its stakeholders, creating uncertain demand, supply-chain, operational, workforce, financial-market, liquidity, and cost risks. Restrictions and changing demand may constrain production or create excess inventory; mitigation and reopening efforts may not suffice and may add costs. The pandemic’s full impact and duration remain uncertain.

nodes.title: Our operating results have in the past fluctuated and may in the future fluctuate, and if our operating results are below the expectations of securities analysts or investors, our stock price could decline.
nodes.summary: Operating results have fluctuated and may continue to do so, so past performance is not a reliable indicator of future results. Factors include limited ability to reduce spending amid multi-year product development, customer-contract compliance, customer payment defaults and credit insurance or bad-debt exposure, unexpected environmental costs, and accounting-standard changes. Missing company, investor, or analyst expectations could cause the stock price to fall or become highly volatile.

nodes.title: Risks Related to Regulatory, Legal, Our Stock and Other Matters Our operations could be affected by the complex laws, rules and regulations to which our business is subject, and political and other actions may adversely impact our business.
nodes.summary: The text describes risks from complex and changing global laws, regulations, and government actions, including compliance costs, penalties, export controls, tariffs, sanctions, geopolitical conflicts, China’s gaming restrictions, and AI-related trade limits. It warns that responsible-AI concerns and evolving ESG expectations may cause liability, reputational damage, added costs, or lost business. It also covers intellectual-property disputes: litigation and enforcement costs, damages or injunctions, countersuits, difficulty obtaining licenses, and possible royalties, cross-licensing, or suspension of product sales.

nodes.title: Regulatory, AI, and ESG Business Risks
key_items: Issues relating to the responsible use of AI in our offerings may result in reputational harm and liability.

Increased scrutiny from shareholders and others regarding our environmental, social and governance responsibilities could result in additional costs or risks and adversely impact our reputation and willingness of customers and suppliers to do business with us.
nodes.summary: Trade and export restrictions, including Chinese limits on gaming and possible regulatory changes, may constrain offerings, delay development or shipments, and harm results. Irresponsible or controversial AI use, inadequate safeguards, or evolving regulation may cause reputational, competitive, legal, and development-cost impacts and slow AI adoption. Rising ESG scrutiny and evolving stakeholder expectations may damage reputation and business relationships, or require added monitoring, reporting, compliance, and other costs.

nodes.title: Actions to adequately protect our IP rights could result in substantial costs to us and our ability to compete could be harmed if we are unsuccessful or if we are prohibited from making or selling our products.
nodes.summary: Protecting IP and handling infringement litigation can be costly, divert personnel, harm operating results, and expose the company to damages, lost profits, invalidated patents, indemnification obligations, countersuits, or injunctions. Infringement may require licenses, royalties, cross-licenses, or suspension or discontinuation of products; acceptable terms may be unavailable. The company relies on legal and contractual protections, but foreign laws may offer weaker protection, increasing piracy and risks from theft or disclosure of trade secrets and employee departures to competitors. It assesses formal protection for innovations but cannot guarantee applications will be approved or protections enforceable.

nodes.title: We are subject to stringent and changing data privacy and security obligations. Privacy concerns relating to our products and services could damage our reputation, deter current and potential users from using our products and services, or result in legal or regulatory proceedings and liability.
nodes.summary: The company faces stringent, evolving privacy and security obligations involving sensitive data, including AI-related use; concerns or data theft, loss, or misuse by the company or partners could harm reputation, operations, and finances, and trigger legal claims or regulatory action. Laws include the GDPR and U.K. GDPR, proposed EU AI regulation, cross-border transfer and localization rules, and U.S. federal and state laws such as the CCPA, CPRA, Virginia CDPA, and Colorado Privacy Act. Compliance may require costly operational and technology changes; failures could lead to fines, litigation, oversight, processing bans, or data destruction orders.

nodes.title: We have exposure to tax liabilities and our operating results may be adversely impacted by higher than expected tax rates.
nodes.summary: As a multinational, the company faces income and other taxes in the U.S. and abroad, complex allocation judgments, and ongoing audits, including IRS examinations for 2018–2019 and audits in Germany, Israel, and India. Tax authority disputes or changes to tax laws—including the TCJA’s R&D amortization rules, proposed U.S. rate and minimum-tax changes, and global minimum-tax initiatives—could raise tax obligations, alter operations, and reduce cash flows and results. Its effective tax rate may also change due to business and profit-location shifts, statutory rates, credits, audit outcomes, accounting and tax-return adjustments, nondeductible expenses, deferred taxes, stock compensation, acquisitions, income levels, organizational changes, and audit settlements or statute expirations, potentially reducing net income.

nodes.title: Our business is exposed to the risks associated with litigation, investigations and regulatory proceedings.
nodes.summary: The text outlines risks from ongoing and future litigation, investigations, and changing regulations, including an appealed securities class action and potential costs, penalties, injunctions, and operational disruption. It describes $11 billion in notes and a $575 million commercial-paper program, with refinancing, debt-service, covenant, credit-rating, and business-flexibility risks. Delaware law, corporate governance provisions, and Microsoft’s rights may impede takeovers. Staff comments are not applicable. NVIDIA describes its Santa Clara headquarters and other U.S. and international facilities as suitable, with lease details referenced elsewhere; legal proceedings are also cross-referenced.

NVIDIA’s accelerated-computing business grew from PC graphics into areas including AI, gaming, science, data centers, and robotics; it has Graphics and Compute & Networking segments and is headquartered in Santa Clara. nodes.title: Supply
nodes.summary: Long manufacturing lead times require uncertain demand forecasts and can cause shortages or excess inventory. The company may build ahead for anticipated growth or pent-up demand that fails to materialize. In fiscal 2022 it broadened its supply base but expects constraints through the first half of fiscal 2023, mainly in Gaming and Networking. It has used non-cancellable advance orders, premiums, and deposits to secure supply; these may create excess inventory or charges if demand falls, shifts to competitors, or product designs change. Demand may disappear before delivery, and uneven supply or production can alter expected revenue and cash flows.

nodes.title: COVID-19
Fiscal Year 2022 Summary
nodes.summary: COVID-19 continued in fiscal 2022, with most employees working remotely and most business travel paused. Gaming, Data Center and Professional Visualization benefited from increased demand related to working, learning and playing at home; Professional Visualization also benefited from hybrid-work workstation demand. Office reopenings are expected to add costs. Uncertainty around customer demand, supply chains, logistics, component availability and inflation could materially harm results. Existing cash, securities and commercial paper are expected to meet liquidity needs. The text then lists fiscal 2022 summary metrics—revenue, gross margin, operating expenses, operating income, net income and diluted earnings per share—and begins a year-ended January 31, 2021 table.

nodes.title: January 30, 2022
nodes.summary: NVIDIA’s fiscal 2022 revenue rose 61% to $26.91 billion across Gaming, Data Center, Professional Visualization, Automotive, and OEM/Other. Gaming growth reflected Ampere GPUs, new games, increased gaming and remote-work demand, and cryptocurrency mining; mining-related demand is difficult to measure and exposed to crypto volatility despite LHR GPUs. Data Center grew 58% on AI and cloud workloads; Professional Visualization rose 100% with Ampere products and hybrid-work demand; Automotive grew 6% on self-driving and AI cockpit solutions; OEM/Other rose 84%, mainly from $550 million in CMP sales, which fell sharply in Q4. Gross margin increased 260 basis points; operating expenses rose 27%. Operating income reached $10.04 billion, net income $9.75 billion, and diluted EPS $3.85, up 122%, 125%, and 123%. Cash and securities totaled $21.21 billion, aided by operating cash flow and $5 billion in debt proceeds; dividends paid were $399 million.

nodes.title: Market Platform Highlights
nodes.summary: The text highlights NVIDIA’s fiscal 2022 platform announcements: Omniverse Enterprise, 65 software development kits, Quantum-2 networking, and Jetson AGX Orin; Gaming updates to GeForce RTX 30, its RTX ecosystem, planned Unity DLSS integration, and a GeForce NOW tier; Data Center GPUs, certified systems, Grace CPU, AI software, and the Earth-2 climate supercomputer; Professional Visualization RTX workstations and Omniverse tools; and Automotive DRIVE Atlan, numerous vehicle and autonomous-driving design wins, a Jaguar Land Rover partnership, and DRIVE Hyperion manufacturing partners.

nodes.title: Critical Accounting Policies and Estimates

Shares and certain other foreign assets held abroad may also be subject to a foreign financial assets tax; participants should consult a personal tax adviser.

title: JAPAN
summary: Japanese residents must report foreign assets, including plan shares, when their total net fair market value exceeds ¥50,000,000 on December 31, and should consult a tax advisor. Acquiring shares worth more than ¥100,000,000 in one transaction requires filing a Securities Acquisition Report with the Ministry of Finance through the Bank of Japan within 20 days; consult a tax advisor about obligations.

title: KOREA
summary:
KOREA
Notifications
Foreign Asset/Account Reporting Information. title: MALAYSIA
summary: For Malaysia, the provision replaces the applicable prior privacy consent and obtains voluntary consent to collect, use, transfer, retain, and process personal and equity-plan data solely to administer participation. Data may be shared with the company, service recipient, affiliates, Schwab, and current or future providers, including recipients abroad whose privacy protections may differ. Participants may request recipient details, access or correct data, ask about processing, or refuse or withdraw consent in writing without cost; employment is unaffected, but future awards and plan administration may be unavailable. Contact NVIDIA-StockAdmin@nvidia.com for consequences. Malaysian Affiliate directors must notify the Affiliate in writing within 14 days of acquiring or disposing of an interest in the company or an affiliate.

title: MEXICO

nodes.title: Terms and Conditions
nodes.summary: Mexican terms require award acceptance to confirm receipt, review, and acceptance of the Plan and Agreement, including express acknowledgment that participation is voluntary, discretionary, creates no acquired right or compensation claim, and carries no company responsibility for share-value decreases. The Company alone administers the Plan; participation is commercial, not employment or service with the Company, and creates no rights or benefits with NVIDIA Mexico or changes to its service terms. The Company may amend or end participation without liability, and the participant releases the Company and related parties from claims for compensation or damages.

nodes.title: Spanish Translation
nodes.summary: Al aceptar el premio, el participante confirma haber recibido y revisado el Plan y el Contrato, acepta sus disposiciones y aprueba expresamente la Sección 11: la participación no es un derecho adquirido, es voluntaria y discrecional; no genera derecho a compensación por la concesión o pérdida del premio; y la Compañía y sus afiliadas no responden por la disminución del valor de las acciones. La Compañía, ubicada en California, administra el Plan, pero la participación no crea una relación laboral ni derechos o beneficios frente a NVIDIA Mexico, único proveedor de servicios, ni altera las condiciones de servicio continuo. La Compañía puede modificar o terminar la participación sin responsabilidad. El participante renuncia a reclamaciones por compensación o daños relacionados con el Plan y otorga una liberación amplia a la Compañía y sus afiliadas y representantes.

summary: The page notes that the Netherlands has no country-specific provisions. In Poland, transfers over €15,000 (or PLN 15,000 for business activity) must use a Polish bank account; foreign-exchange documents must be kept for five years; and quarterly National Bank of Poland reporting is required when foreign-held plan shares and/or cash exceed PLN 7 million. Participants should consult legal advisers.

title: RUSSIA
summary: Russia: RSU acceptance forms a U.S.-completed agreement governed by Delaware law. The award and shares are not registered or offered publicly in Russia; shares may be held with a U.S. broker but not delivered in Russia or sold directly to Russian individuals. Exchange-control repatriation and account-routing rules, exemptions, possible penalties, and a recommendation to seek advice are described. Offshore brokerage accounts may require annual reporting and opening, closing, or change notifications. Holding shares after involuntary termination disqualifies recipients from unemployment benefits. Participation requires acknowledgment of data-privacy terms and any requested consent. Saudi Arabia: distribution is restricted, the regulator disclaims responsibility, and investors should conduct due diligence or consult an adviser. Singapore: the award relies on a securities-law exemption; directors of local affiliates have specified written notification duties, potentially including CEOs.

title: Data Privacy and Saudi Arabia and Singapore Notices
summary: Participants outside the EU/EEA, Switzerland, and UK consent to data processing and transfer and may need to provide additional consent to participate. Saudi Arabia restricts document distribution, disclaims regulatory responsibility for its accuracy, and advises independent due diligence and financial advice. Singapore awards rely on a securities-law exemption and the Plan is not registered as a prospectus. Singapore Affiliate directors, and potentially CEOs, must report specified interests, changes, or appointments in writing within two business days, regardless of residence or employment.

title: SOUTH AFRICA
summary: For South African employees, upon vesting and settlement of the Award, they must promptly report realized income to the Service Recipient; failure may result in a fine. They are responsible for any tax owed beyond amounts withheld. They must also comply with South African exchange control laws and are advised to consult a personal legal advisor.

title: SPAIN
summary: Spain-specific terms state that accepting the award confirms Plan participation and receipt of the Plan; the grant is discretionary, gratuitous, not employment compensation or a guaranteed benefit, and depends on continued active service. Participation generally ends immediately upon service termination for any reason other than death, including dismissal, changed conditions, or company breach. The award is not a Spanish public securities offering or registered prospectus. Share acquisitions and sales require DGCI statistical reporting via D-6, generally each January, or within one month above €1,502,530; some foreign securities accounts must also be reported to the Bank of Spain. Foreign assets exceeding €50,000 per asset type must be reported annually, with later reporting triggered by increases over €20,000; vested shares count, unvested awards do not.

title: SWEDEN
summary: Sweden: Award acceptance authorizes the company or service recipient to withhold or sell deliverable shares to cover tax-related items, even when withholding is not legally required. Switzerland: The private Award offer is unregistered, is not a FinSA prospectus, cannot be publicly distributed or made available beyond employees, and has not been submitted to or approved or supervised by Swiss reviewers or regulators. Taiwan: Plan participation is limited to company and affiliate consultants, directors, and employees and is not a public securities offer; residents may remit up to US$5 million yearly without justification, while transactions of TWD 500,000 or more require a bank form and supporting documents, and legal advice is recommended. Thailand: Single transactions of at least US$1 million from share sales or dividends generally must be repatriated immediately, subject to exemptions; repatriated currency must be converted or deposited within 360 days, with transaction details reported to an authorized bank agent, and individuals are responsible for compliance.

title: Swiss, Taiwan, and Thailand Award Notifications
summary: The page notes that shares may be withheld or sold to cover tax items. Switzerland’s award is a private offering, not a FinSA prospectus, public distribution, or subject to Swiss review or approval. Taiwan limits plan participation to company-affiliated consultants, directors, and employees; residents may remit up to US$5 million annually, with forms and documents required for single transactions of TWD 500,000 or more. In Thailand, proceeds of US$1 million or more per transaction generally must be repatriated immediately, then converted or deposited within 360 days, with transaction details reported; individuals are responsible for compliance.

title: Equity Plan Notices for Turkey, Ukraine, and Dubai
summary: Turkey: The award is a private offering for employees or consultants; grants and vesting occur outside Turkey. Foreign-securities transactions must use a licensed intermediary and be reported to regulators, with compliance the participant’s responsibility. Ukraine: Participants are responsible for exchange-control compliance and should seek legal advice before opening foreign accounts or trading shares. Dubai: The plan is limited to eligible service providers; recipients should conduct due diligence and consult an authorized adviser if needed. UAE authorities have not reviewed, verified, or approved the documents and disclaim responsibility.

title: UNITED KINGDOM
summary: For UK residents, restricted stock units must be settled only in Common Stock, never cash. Participants are responsible for all related taxes and must pay them when requested and indemnify the Company and Service Recipient for amounts paid or withheld on their behalf. Directors and executive officers may be unable to indemnify unpaid income tax if that would constitute a loan; tax unpaid within 90 days after the relevant UK tax year may become a taxable benefit, with the participant responsible for self-assessment income tax and reimbursing applicable National Insurance Contributions.
